item.title: Making the sculpture garden
item.content:
In this part you'll follow the whole process of making a brutalist sculpture garden in Blender: a concrete courtyard with round skylights, a planter with a sculpture in it, and a lettered sign, lit by the sun through the skylights. The video blocks out the space, sets up a camera at eye height, gives everything PBR materials from texture packs, models the sculpture from icospheres and curves, and adds 3D text. Then it renders an afternoon image, finishes it in Photoshop, and lights and renders an evening version. It's a long video, so use the timestamps to jump to the stage you need. Your garden doesn't have to look like this one: take the techniques and design your own. It helps to have watched Part 1 (the Principled BSDF, Node Wrangler, displacement and the Sky Texture). The video uses Blender 4.2 on a Mac, Cycles and Photoshop 2024.

Block out the space

  1. Make the ground. 0:45 The video uses the default cube: in the sidebar (N), set its Dimensions to 30 m by 30 m (and thin), then apply the scale with Ctrl+A 1:00. Build at real-world scale as you go.

  2. Add a roof and cut a skylight. 1:26 Add a plane for part of the roof, raised above the ground. Add a cylinder where you want the hole 2:10, then on the roof add a Boolean modifier (Generate → Boolean) with the cylinder as its object 2:27, and hide the cylinder in the Outliner. Light can now pass through the hole.

  3. Keep the cutters tidy. 3:12 Duplicate the cylinder before you hide it: the copy becomes the skylight's ring. Rename the original "cutter cylinder" and put it in a hidden collection called "cutters" 3:56.

  4. Make the skylight's ring. 3:26 On the copy, named "ring", delete the faces you don't need so it's an open band, scale it down in Z 4:12, add a Solidify modifier for thickness and a Bevel 4:24. Apply the scale before going further 4:42, then set the thickness and make the bevel smaller. Bevels make things look real 4:56. A Subdivision Surface modifier smooths it 5:03; scale the ring up a little so it overlaps the facets of the hole in the roof 5:25.

  5. Fix the shading with Harden Normals. 5:42 Give the bevel 3 segments. Shade Auto Smooth gives odd shading here, and Shade Smooth on its own smooths everything too much, so in the Bevel modifier open Shading and tick Harden Normals 5:56. Now the ring looks like a built feature 6:11.

  6. Make a planter for the focal point. 7:48 The focal point goes right under the skylight. Duplicate the cutter cylinder again, put it in a new collection, "architecture", and call it "floor ring" 8:15. Add an edge loop 9:32, select the ring of faces around the side (Alt+Shift+click; the video uses Option+Shift on a Mac) and extrude it out with E then S 9:44. Then select the top face, extrude it down and scale it in to make a dish 10:02.

  7. Build the walls. 10:41 Add a cube and shape it into a wall (the on-screen gizmos help). Duplicate it with Shift+D for the opposite wall 11:11, then select both, duplicate them, press Esc to leave the copies in place and rotate them with R Z 90: four walls 11:16.

  8. Set the walls to a real height. 15:16 Before adding textures, the scale should be 1, so apply it. The video removes parts of the walls it doesn't need 15:36, then sets their height to 3.5 m in Dimensions (between 3 and 4 m) 16:28. With snapping set to Vertex, drag a wall up along the blue axis and hover over a corner to sit it exactly in place 16:36. Match the other walls to 3.5 m and apply their scale 17:01.

Light the space with a sky

6:27 Light the space early, so you design with the light in mind.

  1. Switch to Cycles. 6:27 Set the render engine to Cycles with GPU Compute. If your computer struggles with the rendered view, work in Material Preview instead 6:35.

  2. Add a Sky Texture. 6:48 Turn off the default light, then in the Shading workspace switch the Shader Editor to World and add a Sky Texture 7:01. Turn Sun Disc on to get crisp shadows, and set the sun's elevation so the sun is almost straight overhead the focal point (the video uses about 90°) 7:57.

  3. Tone it down. 27:23 With the sun disc on, the scene is very bright. The video lowers Sun Intensity to 0.25 and changes the elevation 27:34; for the final afternoon render it uses an elevation of 135° and a rotation of 205° 1:21:43, so the sun comes in at an angle through the skylights.

Set up the camera

  1. Lock the camera to the view. 11:31 Look through the camera and lock it to the view (Lock Camera to View), so you can move it by navigating.

  2. Keep it at eye height. 11:39 Build at real-world scale and place the camera where a person would stand. Add an empty near the camera 12:00 and set its Location Z to 1.6 m, about eye height 12:27. Then select the camera, open the Object Constraint tab and add a Copy Location constraint with the empty as its Target, with only Z ticked 12:53. Now the camera can move around and look up and down, but always from 1.6 m 13:43.

  3. Use a wide lens. 13:30 The video sets the camera's focal length to 22 mm, a wide angle. If navigating gets awkward, View → Frame Selected resets it 14:15.

Materials for the architecture

18:43 All the texture packs are added with Node Wrangler's Add Principled Setup, as in Part 1. If you haven't enabled Node Wrangler, do it in Edit → Preferences → Add-ons (search for "node") 19:02.

  1. Give the planter its own surface. 19:22 In Edit Mode, duplicate the planter's inner face (Shift+D), separate it (Mesh → Separate → By Loose Parts) and move it into place, slightly larger 19:39. Give it a new material and pack its UVs to use the whole texture space (Pack Islands in the UV Editor) 20:10.

  2. Make the planter look built. 20:37 Real things aren't computer-perfect, which is why everything gets bevels. Add a Subdivision Surface modifier and Shade Smooth 20:56. If scaling goes strangely, the origin is in the wrong place: Object → Set Origin moves it back to the geometry 21:31. Add supporting edges to keep it flat where it should be 21:49: places where shadows can form and ambient occlusion can gather make it look built 23:25.

  3. Add a ground texture. 23:49 Select the planter's surface, press Shift+W and choose Add Principled Setup. The video uses Ground 037 from ambientCG.com 24:13. Save the file before setting up displacement 24:31.

  4. Set up displacement. 24:50 Set the Feature Set to Experimental, add a Subdivision Surface modifier and tick Adaptive Subdivision (optional). The round face was an n-gon and the texture stretched badly 25:13, so the video rebuilds it as quads, starting with Merge at Center and dissolving edges (there are several ways to fill a circle with quads) 25:36. Then it's much less distorted 26:26. Turn on displacement in the material's Settings → Surface → Displacement and Bump 26:48. At the default scale it's far too strong: set the Displacement node's Scale to 0.02, or even 0.01 26:58.

  5. Add concrete to the planter. 28:00 Add a new material from the Shader Editor (or the Material tab) 28:06, use Add Principled Setup again and pick a concrete (Concrete 042A) 28:28. The texture is badly mapped, so unwrap the planter with UV → Smart UV Project and check for visible seams 29:04. Enable displacement and adaptive subdivision for it too 29:49.

  6. Make the ground less flat. 30:51 Turn on proportional editing, select a vertex in the planter's surface and press G Z, using the scroll wheel to change the area it affects 31:04. For more vertices to work with, select everything, right-click and choose Subdivide: you can almost sculpt it 31:35. Less perfect is what you want 32:11.

  7. Texture the floor. 47:26 Select the ground, use Add Principled Setup with another concrete (Concrete 031) 48:18, and apply the scale. The texture is far too big for a 30 m floor: in the Mapping node, raise Scale so it tiles (the video tries 4, 8 and 10, and settles on 16) 48:42. Turn on displacement at 0.01 49:27.

  8. Darken the floor, lighten the planter. 49:41 Mix the ambient occlusion map into the floor's color and add a Hue/Saturation/Value node to bring its value down 49:45. For the planter, do the same the other way 50:17: a Mix Color node set to Multiply with the ambient occlusion in the B slot and Factor at 1 50:29, then a Hue/Saturation/Value node with the value up. White concrete on a dark concrete floor separates them by value 50:45.

  9. Name the materials. 51:04 Light concrete, dark concrete, grass, brass (or rose gold) and pink plastic, so you can pick them from the list 51:18.

  10. Concrete for the roof and the skylight ring. 52:11 Turn on the Face Orientation overlay to check which way the roof faces (red shows the back of a face). Rather than flipping it, the video adds a Solidify modifier 52:28 and gives the roof the light concrete. The skylight ring gets the light concrete too 53:09. Its texture is warped, so apply its Solidify (in Object Mode), move its Bevel above the Subdivision Surface 53:35 and use Smart UV Project 53:59. That leaves a seam where the camera can see it 54:12, so mark seams yourself (U → Mark Seam) where the camera won't see them, and unwrap 55:07.

  11. Texture the walls. 1:08:43 The walls get the dark concrete. In the UV Editing workspace, scale each wall's UVs so the concrete's squares match the size of the squares on the other surfaces 1:09:13, and move them to line up the seams 1:10:09. Give the walls a Solidify and bevels too, with Shade Smooth and Harden Normals 1:10:39; keep the bevel small 1:11:30. Material Preview helps line up textures 1:12:41.

    The video adds View → Frame Selected to Quick Favorites (right-click it, Add to Quick Favorites), so pressing Q always gets back to the selected object 1:13:43.

  12. Make a material unique. 1:18:46 For the roof's edge, click the number of users beside the material's name (light concrete has 4) to make a separate copy, and name it "light concrete roof" 1:19:06.

    Adaptive subdivision only works as the last modifier in the stack 1:20:47. On the roof, that put it after the Boolean and the skylight's hole disappeared, so the video leaves the roof without it 1:21:19.

Make the sculpture

  1. Start with a cone. 32:30 Add a basic shape in the planter: a cone, which will be metal. Give it a new material and Add Principled Setup with a metal pack (Metal 057B) 32:55. Its displacement is so subtle it isn't worth the render time, so the video deletes it 33:36.

  2. Push the colour. 33:56 The copper colour isn't convincing in this light, so add a Hue/Saturation/Value node after the color map and raise Saturation 34:22.

  3. Add spheres and think about composition. 35:13 Add some icospheres. Where the large, medium and small objects go matters 35:48, and lines draw the eye in 36:00.

  4. Make stems from curves. 37:53 Add a Bézier curve and rotate it upright to use as a stem. In Edit Mode, with snapping to Vertex, snap its end to the cone 38:18. In the curve's Object Data properties, give Geometry → Bevel some Depth to turn it into a pipe, and raise its resolution 39:35. Duplicate it for the other spheres, shaping each one differently 40:15.

    If points you move drag others with them, proportional editing is still on from earlier. It's easy to leave on by accident 39:14.

  5. Refine the shapes. 41:50 Check the silhouette from the camera view and reshape stems you don't like 42:07. For more control points and a smoother curve, select the points and choose Segments → Subdivide 42:59. Put the sculpture's parts in their own collection (the video calls it "plop art") 43:25.

  6. Share the copper material. 44:41 Select the stems, then the cone last, press Ctrl+L (the video uses Cmd+L on a Mac) and choose Link Materials 44:53.

  7. Make the spheres glossy pink plastic. 45:16 Give the spheres a new material: pink, with low roughness. To keep their facets without looking too perfect, apply their scale and add a Bevel modifier 45:52. If it does nothing, set Limit Method to None: the angle limit was stopping it 46:11. Raise the amount, use 3 segments and tick Harden Normals 46:31: smoothed, but still faceted.

  8. Copy the modifiers. 46:59 Apply the scale on the other spheres, select the bevelled one last and choose Copy Modifiers from the same Ctrl+L menu 47:07.

Add lettering

  1. Add text. 56:02 Press Shift+A and choose Text. Stand it up: hold Ctrl while rotating to snap, or type 90° in the sidebar 56:28. To change the words, go into Edit Mode, delete the text and type 56:50.

  2. Give it depth. 57:14 In the text's Object Data properties, raise Geometry → Extrude for solid block letters 57:27. The video builds a sign for it from a cube 57:48, sits it on the floor by snapping to the floor's face 59:11, and bevels it like everything else 59:34. (Ctrl+Space maximizes the area you're working in 58:23.)

  3. Space the letters. 1:00:39 Under the text's Paragraph → Spacing, Line Spacing and Character Spacing tighten or loosen it. Blender can't adjust the kerning between particular letters; for that, make the text in Illustrator and bring it in as an SVG, or convert it to a mesh 1:01:16.

  4. Make metal letters. 1:01:37 Give the text a new material, "metal text": metallic and dark. Add a small Geometry → Bevel so the edges catch highlights 1:01:58. Setting Fill Mode to None gives cut-out metal outlines; duplicate the text (Shift+D, Esc), give the copy a front fill and slide it forward for fabricated-looking letters 1:02:24. Check the metal's roughness too 1:03:10.

  5. Shape the sign. 1:04:28 Add edge loops with Ctrl+R (the video uses Cmd+R) and scale the bottom ones; Shift+Z while scaling leaves Z alone and scales only X and Y 1:04:47. Give the sign the light concrete 1:05:45. The video also changes "Brutal" to "Brutalist", the style it's going for 1:07:12.

Composition and revisions

  • 1:15:02 Look through the camera to decide where to take the picture from. A roof piece that hangs over the top looks good but unrealistic, so the video gives it thickness and bevels to make it make sense 1:15:18.
  • 1:27:54 After the first render, the video notices that "sculpture" is misspelled, and critiques the image while it has to re-render anyway: the sign is too big for the space and the text takes up too much room 1:28:26.
  • 1:30:17 The revised design, made off camera, puts the lettering on the wall, spaced out, where it makes good use of the shadows. Two more skylights bring more light down and repeat the ring as an architectural motif, which wouldn't make sense only once 1:30:29.

Render the afternoon image

  1. Set the output. 1:22:35 In the Output properties, render at 1920 × 1080; set the percentage to 200% for a larger image (2K or 4K) 1:22:46. Set File Format to OpenEXR, half float, RGBA 1:22:56. (You can also choose the format when you save from the render window.)

  2. Set the samples. 1:23:30 The video renders with 4096 samples, the default, and the denoiser. If your graphics card can't manage that many, rely on the denoiser, or let the render run overnight; the video wouldn't go over about 4000 1:23:50.

  3. Render and save. 1:24:05 Choose Render → Render Image. When it's done, choose Image → Save As in the render window, name it (the video uses "sculpture garden") and save it as OpenEXR, half, RGBA 1:24:18.

  4. Open it in Photoshop. 1:24:45 It's a 32-bit image (Image → Mode). Lower the exposure and the blown-out sky's blue comes back; raise it and there's a little more detail in the darks 1:25:04.

  5. Tone it with HDR Toning. 1:25:36 In the HDR Toning dialog, shape the curve to change the lows, mids and highs, mapping it to where most of the colour information is 1:26:08.

  6. Add a look and a vignette. 1:26:21 Add a Color Lookup adjustment layer (the video likes Kodak 5218) 1:26:29. For a vignette, add a black Solid Color layer, fill an ellipse with black on its mask (Ctrl+D to deselect; Cmd+D on a Mac), feather the mask, lower its opacity and put it under the lookup so the lookup applies to it 1:27:04.

  7. Re-render and finish. 1:31:39 After the revisions, re-render and save a new EXR (the + button beside the name numbers it) 1:31:48. Run HDR Toning again (your curve may look very different: keep the highlights bright and some sky, and cut the grey wash in the lows) 1:33:12, then drag the Color Lookup and vignette layers onto the new image 1:33:51. For grain, fill a layer, add Filter → Noise → Add Noise, set it to Multiply under the other layers at a low opacity 1:34:49. Export it as a PNG (Quick Export as PNG) 1:35:53.

Light the evening

  1. Lower the sun. 1:36:33 Duplicate the Sky Texture node and plug the copy into the Background 1:36:42. Set the sun's elevation just under 180°, at the horizon (the video uses 178°) 1:36:58: warm light hits the walls. Raise the intensity to 1 1:37:15.

  2. Light the sculpture with spotlights. 1:37:29 Add a spot light (Shift+A) aimed up at the sculpture, a warm light of about 300 W 1:38:12. For the colour, you can use nodes: click Use Nodes in the light's properties, which drives the light with an Emission node, and plug a Blackbody node into its colour 1:38:20. Household lights run from about 2700 K to 5000 K; 2700 K is warm 1:38:52. The video sets the strength to 2 for now 1:39:20.

  3. Soften and add more. 1:39:38 Raise the light's Radius for softer shadows. Duplicate it, move the copy and rotate it on Z so each light points at the sculpture 1:39:44; looking straight down makes it easier 1:40:18. The video uses three in front and one behind 1:40:33, with a second viewport set to the camera's rendered view to check them 1:40:48, angles one down so it doesn't light the ceiling 1:41:26, and lowers the strength to 1 1:42:10.

  4. Make a ground light. 1:43:07 For lights along the edges, add a circle, fill it in Edit Mode, extrude it up, then out (E then S), then down (E Z) 1:43:47. Give it a dark metallic material, then add a second material slot with an emissive material: an Emission shader with a Blackbody at 2700 K and a strength of 4, assigned to its top face 1:44:47. Shade it smooth with auto smooth 1:45:52, snap it to the floor's surface and scale it down very small 1:46:04.

  5. Repeat it with an Array. 1:46:23 Apply the scale and add an Array modifier along negative Y 1:46:44. Raise the count to fill the wall (the video uses 20) 1:48:08, then duplicate the row and rotate it for the other walls 1:49:46. They light the bottom of the walls.

  6. Check it with a quick render. 1:50:11 Render at 50% size for a faster preview 1:50:31. The ground lights need to be brighter, so the video raises their emission strength to 60 1:51:08 and reduces their count 1:51:48.

  7. Light the planter. 1:52:10 Make a recessed LED strip under the planter's rim: select a ring of faces, add a material slot, choose the glowing material (named "emissive") and click Assign 1:53:32. It's too bright, so click its number of users to make it a single-user copy, "emissive 2", and lower the strength to 10, then 5 1:54:05. It's too warm too: raise the Blackbody to 3000, then 3500 1:54:40.

Render the evening image

1:55:01 Render, save the EXR and tone it in Photoshop as before 1:55:27. For a night look, the video uses a different Color Lookup, TealOrangePlusContrast, at about 8% opacity, for contrast between the blue and orange 1:56:47.

Wrap-up

You've blocked out a space at real-world scale, cut skylights with Booleans, and made everything look built with bevels and Harden Normals. You've textured it with PBR packs, tuning them with Mapping, ambient occlusion and Hue/Saturation/Value, and made a sculpture from icospheres and curves and a sign from 3D text. You lit it with a Sky Texture for the afternoon and spotlights, emissive ground lights and a glowing strip for the evening, and finished both renders from EXR files in Photoshop 1:57:42. Now build your own garden: adapt whatever's useful 1:57:56.
